notes: The largest single point of contention is scoring g.reachable 3 rather than 5. What docs.stripe.com returns to the 10 retrieval user-agents is not the HTML the browser gets but deliberately prepared markdown (docs-accept 854 B vs 257712 B, docs-connect 3346 B vs 61338 B), and that is precisely an active AI-friendly design — not cloaking, and not a soft block. I read both markdown documents word for word; they are substantively equivalent to the browser version (the browser version of docs-accept is itself only a variant index page). Under v1.1 rule 6, "judge substance, not format", scoring 5 would be entirely defensible. I settled on 3, and the deciding factor was not the format difference but the `x-robots-tag: none` header sent only to retrieval user-agents: the browser does not receive it, GPTBot and PerplexityBot both do, and none = noindex+nofollow, which is a difference at the directive level, not the presentation level. A reader who considers that header a duplicate-indexing safeguard for the markdown variant, and therefore not an inconsistency on the retrieval side, should rescore this check to 5, moving readiness to 79. To be clear: even rescored to 5, the cap still holds, because g.robots independently falls short of full marks.

Scoring g.robots 3 also deserves review. The wildcard group in stripe.com/robots.txt does contain Allow: /docs, which read literally is "an Allow directive is present"; but tier 5 requires "explicitly allows the major retrieval user-agents", and the only user-agents named anywhere in the file are ia_archiver and rogerbot, with the 10 AI retrieval user-agent names appearing 0 times. That Allow is a path exception, not a statement allowing retrieval user-agents. Conversely, the robots.txt on the docs.stripe.com subdomain does carry `Content-Signal: ai-train=yes, search=yes, ai-input=yes` plus `Allow: /`, making it more explicit than the main site — and 2 of the 8 sampled URLs sit on that subdomain. I scored 3 on the main site's terms, ranking hosts by primacy (6 of 8 are on stripe.com, and the audit target is named stripe.com). If the convention were changed to "weight by the host each sampled URL sits on", the conclusion would loosen.

MD5 cannot be used to test content consistency on this site, and that affects anyone attempting to reproduce the audit. For the same URL, any two user-agents (including two that both look like browsers) produce different MD5s, because the page injects a per-request nonce and an edge-experiment id. What I used instead was byte-count difference plus a comparison of extracted body text: on the 6 stripe.com URLs the 10 retrieval user-agents differ from the browser by <1.3%, which I judged consistent. A reviewer using MD5 as a strict equality test would conclude "all 10 user-agents are inconsistent", which would score g.reachable 0 rather than 3 — I consider that the wrong call, but the methodological disagreement has to be stated.

p2.answer-passages scores 7 (half) rather than 9 (most), stuck between 5/8 and 6/8. The only paragraph on docs-accept inside the 25–120 word band is the 41-word aside about the no-code option, and the page intro is only 14 words; home's hero measures 23 words, two words short of the floor. If either of those two pages were judged to pass, the count would be 6/8, "most" would apply, the score would be 9, and readiness would move to 79. The v1.1 calibration record happens to note that scoring svelte 0 for a "39-word core sentence, one word short" was a v1.0 error; the 25-word line will keep producing the same kind of boundary problem — this time I used the boundary itself to rule home out, and a reader has grounds to disagree.

Awarding p2.question-intent the full 7 points involves some leniency. Among the 6/8 that pass, home and blog-aiecon are both borderline: "Financial infrastructure to grow your revenue" and "Mapping the AI economy" are descriptive sentences rather than task sentences or questions, and I counted them under the v1.1 convention of "exclude only pure keyword strings or brand labels". Recognising only harder task sentences or questions would drop the pass count to 4/8 and the check to 5 points. Looking the other way, the titles on payments and billing ("Global Payment Processing Platform", "Recurring Payments & Subscription Solutions") are textbook brand-label-plus-keyword-string, so the two most important commercial pages are precisely the ones that read least like human speech — a structural fact the 7 points should not obscure.

p1.organization scores 6, but Organization+WebSite appears only on the home page; 7 of the 8 sampled pages lack it (payments, docs-accept and docs-connect have 0 ld+json blocks). The check is titled "sitewide" in the rubric, yet the three tier criteria themselves examine only field completeness, logo resolution and sameAs, not the number of pages passing. I scored 6 by the text of the criteria, but scored by the "sitewide" intent of the title, those 6 points should drop at least one tier. p3.video has the same shape: tier 3 requires "sustained output and VideoObject markup on-site", Stripe satisfies the first half and scores 0 on the second, so it can only land on tier 2, whose criterion text reads "sporadic content" — the tier description does not match the facts, which is a problem with the rubric's wording, not with the site.

The 10 questions in p4.question-coverage are ones I wrote myself, which is a source of bias in itself. Stripe's resources library holds thousands of concept pages (the llms.txt directory alone lists 285 entries), so almost any set of concept questions would return high coverage; the one stable gap is vendor head-to-heads (Stripe vs PayPal/Adyen/Square), entirely absent, and questions of that kind are very frequent in AI retrieval. Adding two more comparison questions to the 10 would drop this check from 4 points to 3 or even 2. The score on this check should be reviewed together with the question list; the score alone means nothing.

Finally, the most glaring thing in this report, which has to be stated plainly: the uncapped normalised score is 77 (77/100), at the top of "Solid"; after the cap it is 40, in "Getting started". The entire 38-point gap comes from two gate checks each falling 2 points short, while Stripe's performance at the content layer (self-contained answer passages, title intent, named authors, third-party endorsement, question coverage) is clearly stronger than any of the five sites in our v1.0 sample. I applied the rule as written, but the reader should see both numbers: 77 is where this site actually stands today, and 40 is the rule taking a forced position on the single point that robots.txt does not name AI crawlers as allowed. The cap is the right design for a site crawlers genuinely cannot enter; whether it remains reasonable applied to a site that returns 200 on 80/80, renders all of its body text server-side, and actively serves markdown to AI, is a question v1.2 should answer — the calibration record has already conceded once that "this is not the site's problem, it is the rubric's problem".

citation.note: AI citation performance was not measured this time, so it scores no points and is not folded into readiness. There are two reasons. First, the rubric itself defines it as an outcome metric, determined jointly by readiness and time; the same question asked repeatedly returns different results, it is not reproducible, and folding it into the main score would damage both the client and the credibility of the method. Second, this audit used curl and HTTP headers throughout for off-site, re-checkable observation, and never put a real question to ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews or any other engine, so any "citation rate" number would be one I made up. Measuring it later requires a separate design: 10 fixed real questions from the payments industry, fixed engines and regions, each question repeated 3 times to count hit frequency, and the test time window explicitly recorded — that is a standalone report, not a part of this score.
